# Identification of a Polypeptide Inhibitor of O-GlcNAc Transferase with Picomolar Affinity

## Abstract

O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) is an essential mammalian enzyme that binds thousands of different proteins, including substrates that it glycosylates and nonsubstrate interactors that regulate its biology. OGT also has one proteolytic substrate, the transcriptional coregulator host cell factor 1 (HCF-1), which it cleaves in a process initiated by glutamate side chain glycosylation at a series of central repeats. Although HCF-1 is OGT’s most prominent binding partner, its affinity for the enzyme has not been quantified. Here, we report a time-resolved Förster resonance energy transfer assay to measure ligand binding to OGT and show that an HCF-1-derived polypeptide (HCF3R) binds with picomolar affinity to the enzyme (KD ≤ 85 pM). This high affinity is driven in large part by conserved asparagines in OGT’s tetratricopeptide repeat domain, which form bidentate contacts to the HCF-1 peptide backbone; replacing any one of these asparagines with alanine reduces binding by more than 5 orders of magnitude. Because the HCF-1 polypeptide binds so tightly to OGT, we tested its ability to inhibit enzymatic function. We found that HCF3R potently inhibits OGT both in vitro and in cells and used this finding to develop a genetically encoded, inducible OGT inhibitor that can be degraded with a small molecule, allowing for reversible and tunable inhibition of OGT.

## Introduction

O-GlcNAcylation is a nutrient- and stress-responsive post-translational modification installed exclusively by O-linked N-acetyl-d-glucosamine transferase [O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT)],1−7 an essential mammalian glycosyltransferase.8−10 OGT transfers N-acetyl-d-glucosamine (GlcNAc) onto serine and threonine residues in thousands of nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins (Figure S1A);11,12 these modifications play critical roles in protein stability,13,14 homeostatic signaling,15 and other essential cellular processes including organelle trafficking.16,17 In vertebrates, OGT also has another catalytic activity: it cleaves the transcriptional coregulator host cell factor 1 (HCF-1) at one or more of six conserved proteolytic repeats (Figure S1B).18 HCF-1 is not only a substrate but also OGT’s most common binding partner, with up to 50% of OGT found in complex with it.19−21 HCF-1 cleavage, which occurs via decomposition of an O-GlcNAcylated glutamate intermediate,22,23 may regulate HCF-1’s protein–protein interactions,24,25 and has been linked to cell cycle control.19,26−28

Structural studies have shed some light on how OGT binds HCF-1 and other substrates. OGT contains a C-terminal catalytic domain and an N-terminal domain comprised of 13 tetratricopeptide repeats (TPRs) that form a right-handed superhelix (Figure 1A). The side chains of a ladder of asparagine residues point into the TPR lumen (Figure S2A). TPRs are 34-amino acid helical hairpins typically involved in protein–protein interactions and, consistent with this function, OGT’s TPR domain has been implicated in substrate glycosylation and protein binding in vitro and in cells.20,29,30 A structure of a truncated OGT variant bound to a 26-amino acid HCF-1 proteolytic repeat showed that conserved asparagines in the TPRs proximal to OGT’s active site form bidentate contacts to the amide backbone of the peptide (Figure S2B).22 Biochemical and additional structural studies, including a recent structure of full-length OGT bound to the glycosidase O-GlcNAcase (OGA), have confirmed the importance of these and other asparagine ladder residues in substrate recognition.9,30−32

Despite efforts to characterize how OGT binds its many substrates and partners, there is no quantitative information on binding affinities. Prior efforts to assess OGT’s binding interactions have used qualitative, non-equilibrium methods such as co-immunoprecipitation and affinity capture, or indirect methods such as glycosylation and cleavage assays.22,32,33 These methods and their findings have been informative, but a quantitative assay is still needed to compare binding affinities and quantify the contributions of specific residues in OGT or its substrates to affinity.

Here, we report a time-resolved Förster resonance energy transfer (TR-FRET) equilibrium binding assay that enables quantitative assessment of OGT-substrate interactions. In this study, we used peptides derived from HCF-1 proteolytic repeats as FRET acceptor probes (Figure 1B). In the course of this work, we identified an HCF-1-derived polypeptide that binds with picomolar affinity to OGT. We find that the high-affinity binding is driven by conserved asparagine ladder residues, with individual residues contributing as much as 7 kcal/mol in binding energy. Using closely related model substrates that can undergo either OGT-mediated cleavage or glycosylation, we have also shown that reducing the binding affinity by mutating asparagine ladder residues abrogates cleavage but increases glycosylation. This finding suggests that substrate glycosylation profiles in cells reflect a complex relationship between binding affinities and enzyme turnover. Lastly, we took advantage of the very high affinity of one of our HCF-1-derived peptides to develop a genetically encoded OGT inhibitor, providing a new strategy to probe OGT function.

## Results

### Quantitative Assay to Measure OGT-Substrate Binding Affinities

To characterize substrate binding to OGT, we opted for a TR-FRET approach based on our recently developed CoraFluor technology.34 TR-FRET assays often provide superior sensitivity and robustness over other assay methodologies due to the long-lived fluorescence of the lanthanide metal complexes used as donors. Previous work has established a wide dynamic range with sensitivity for CoraFluors extending into femtomolar concentrations.34 Moreover, the ease of labeling with amine-reactive CoraFluor derivatives enables simple incorporation of the TR-FRET donor species. We labeled an anti-His6 antibody with a CoraFluor-1-pentafluorophenyl (PFP) ester to furnish the FRET donor when combined with polyhistidine-tagged OGT in vitro (Figure S3). To generate a FRET acceptor (probe 1), we expressed and purified a HaloTag fusion of a variant of HCF-1’s second proteolytic repeat bearing a glycosite E10A mutation that prevents catalytic turnover (HCF1R-A), and then labeled the HaloTag with an Alexa Fluor 488 (AF488) functionalized HaloTag ligand (Figure 1D). Using wild-type OGT (OGT-WT) and varying amounts of 1, we conducted a dose–response binding assay in the presence of saturating uridine diphosphate (UDP, 0.1 mM),35 which is produced from UDP-GlcNAc as a byproduct of O-GlcNAcylation. OGT uses an ordered bi-bi mechanism with UDP-GlcNAc binding first and UDP leaving last during the catalytic cycle.33 We used UDP as a proxy for UDP-GlcNAc because the latter can hydrolyze during prolonged incubation with enzyme, leading to heterogeneity in the complexes that form and delaying equilibrium. UDP binds OGT with similar affinity as UDP-GlcNAc and forms many of the same contacts to peptide substrates.33,35 After background correction using samples containing no OGT, we obtained a hyperbolic curve consistent with specific binding of 1 and an equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of 450 nM (Figure 1E).

### Multirepeat HCF-1 Substrates Bind OGT with Picomolar Affinity

The 26-mer HCF1R polypeptide represents only one of six conserved proteolytic repeats in the protein HCF-1. Previous work has demonstrated that OGT cannot cleave HCF1R, although it readily cleaves longer HCF-1 repeat substrates, including HCF3R, which is composed of the first three proteolytic repeats and their spanning regions.18 The fact that HCF3R can be cleaved but HCF1R cannot has been attributed to additional contacts that increase residence time in OGT’s active site.23,33,36 We purified two HCF3R variants, one with wild-type E10 glycosites (HCF3R-EEE) and one with E10A catalytic-dead mutations in all three repeats (HCF3R-AAA). We then conducted a competition binding assay for these two HCF3R substrates and OGT-WT using 1 at its KD and saturating UDP. HCF3R-EEE and HCF3R-AAA bound OGT-WT with KD,app values of 13.2 and 1.7 nM, respectively (Figure S4). Given that we used 1 nM OGT in this assay, the obtained KD,app for HCF3R-AAA is close to the assay floor and may be an underestimate of its affinity.

To obtain a more accurate KD in a saturation binding assay, we purified HCF3R-AAA fused at its N-terminus to HaloTag, which we labeled with AF488-tetrafluorophenyl (TFP) ester to produce probe 2 (Figure 2A). We opted for this labeling method to introduce more fluorophores into the probe (∼2 AF488/protein), anticipating the need for improved signal to compensate for the low enzyme concentrations necessary to achieve a more sensitive binding affinity measurement.37 Moreover, the lack of lysine residues in the HCF3R sequence enabled nonspecific labeling with low risk of impacting probe binding to OGT. We performed binding assays using 2 in the presence of saturating UDP, as before. Using 250 pM OGT-WT in an attempt to lower our assay floor and exit the titration regime for 2, and an equilibration time of ∼24 h, we obtained a KD,app of 85 pM [95% confidence interval: (63–114 pM)], close to half the OGT concentration (Figure 2B). This result suggested that HCF3R titrates OGT. We attempted to reduce the OGT concentration further, but our attempts to extract meaningful data were hampered by decreased signal and increased noise. Thus, 85 pM may represent an upper bound for the KD of 2 for OGT. Given that HCF3R is a long (125 residues), unstructured peptide containing few charged or entropically restrictive residues (e.g., proline), its picomolar affinity for OGT is notable.

We also measured the off-rate for 2, obtaining a koff of 0.00038 s–1 and a corresponding t1/2 of 31 min (Figure S5). Applying an analysis described by Jarmoskaite et al., the system reached equilibrium approximately 2.5 h after mixing at the lowest concentrations in our saturation assay.37 Thus, under our assay conditions, probe 2 reached equilibrium by the time of measurement. We attempted a similar analysis with probe 1, but found that signal had nearly fully decayed by the time measurement began (∼40 s after addition of competitor ligand), suggesting a short half-life (t1/2 ≤ 20 s) and equilibration in minutes for competition binding assays.

### Active Site Cofactor Occupancy Promotes Tight Binding of HCF3R

With OGT ligands and a binding assay in hand, we were positioned to interrogate factors that control the interaction between OGT and its substrates. We first examined the role of the UDP cofactor in promoting interactions between OGT and its substrates. Structural studies have shown that the nucleotide portion of the cofactor substrate binds beneath the peptide substrate in the OGT active site and helps to orient the peptide substrate for glycosylation by using its α-phosphate to form a hydrogen bond to the glycosite residue’s backbone amide.22,33 Although the structures imply that the cofactor is important in peptide binding, its contribution to the affinity of peptide substrates for OGT has not been measured.

To quantify the effects of the cofactor on substrate binding, we repeated our saturation binding assay with OGT-WT and 2, but without the addition of UDP. Under these conditions, we obtained a KD of 52 nM (Figure 2C), which is consistent with a change in free energy of at least 3.6 kcal/mol when compared to the affinity measured in the presence of UDP and provides evidence of a substrate-dependent binding mode. Probe 1 has a much lower affinity (KD = 450 nM, Figure 1E), and we estimate that its KD for OGT would be ∼200 μM without cofactor-driven contributions. We conclude that contacts to the nucleotide cofactor play a pivotal role in substrate engagement by OGT, consistent with the idea that OGT “senses” cofactor concentration, which it transduces into binding and glycosylation activities.

### Replacing Single TPR Asparagines with Alanines Reduces Ligand Binding Affinity by More than 5 Orders of Magnitude

OGT employs conserved asparagine side chains to anchor the HCF-1 peptide backbone in the TPR lumen (Figures 3A and S2).22,31 Structures of OGT bound to HCF1R show that the N322, N356, N390, and N424 side chain amides form bidentate hydrogen bonds to alternating HCF-1 residues, while N458 forms a single hydrogen bond. We individually substituted all five asparagine ladder residues in OGT’s proximal lumen with alanine and tested binding of probe 2 to each variant. We also tested the OGT variant 5N5A-1, in which all five asparagine to alanine substitutions are made.30,31 Of the six variants tested, only OGT-N458A still bound tightly to 2 (KD,app = 1 nM) (Figure 3B). The N322A variant showed partial binding at the highest tested concentration (20% at 1 μM), while binding of 2 to OGT variants N356A, N390A, and N424A was undetectable. Size exclusion chromatography profiles showed that the hydrodynamic behavior of the OGT asparagine mutants was unaltered by replacing asparagine side chains in the TPR lumen with alanine (Figure S6). Moreover, a previous study from our lab showed that the helical content of the quintuple asparagine mutant is unchanged.31 Therefore, the changes in affinity likely do not reflect gross structural changes in OGT. Although we expected the asparagines that form bidentate contacts to the HCF-1 probe to make larger contributions to binding than N458, we were surprised by the magnitude. The KD for probe 2 binding to OGT variants N356A, N390A, and N424A is estimated to be >10 μM, which is at least 5 orders of magnitude weaker than its KD for OGT-WT. This change in binding affinity corresponds to a free energy change (ΔΔG°) of more than 7 kcal/mol, a remarkable change for removal of a single amino acid side chain.38

### Asparagine Ladder Substitutions Reduce HCF-1 Cleavage but Can Increase Glycosylation

Given the dramatic effect on binding affinity, we wondered how the single asparagine substitutions would affect OGT’s ability to cleave HCF3R or to glycosylate a closely related peptide. We tested cleavage of the wild-type polypeptide HCF3R-EEE by all five asparagine to alanine variants using OGT-WT and OGT-5N5A-1 as positive and negative controls, respectively. Cleavage products were visualized by Coomassie staining after SDS-PAGE (Figure 3C). Of the variants, only OGT-N458A had robust cleavage activity, almost completely consuming the starting material over 3 h like OGT-WT. OGT-N322A had low but detectable cleavage activity; cleavage by the remaining single asparagine mutants was not detected. Therefore, for HCF3R, higher cleavage activity directly correlates with binding affinity for OGT.

We tested the impact of binding affinity on glycosylation using a model substrate, HCF3R-SAA, which is an HCF3R variant with an E10S mutation in the first repeat and E10A mutations in the second and third repeats, resulting in a substrate that cannot be cleaved, but can be glycosylated at a single position.22 Glycosylated product was detected by western blotting (Figure 3D). O-GlcNAcylation was undetectable compared to the no-treatment control for wild-type OGT and OGT-N458A, and low for OGT-N322A; however, the reactions with OGT variants N356A, N390A, N424A, and 5N5A-1 resulted in strong bands for glycosylated HCF3R. Therefore, glycosylation activity is inversely correlated with binding affinity for this substrate. We attribute the negligible glycosylation by wild-type OGT and OGT-N458A to low turnover caused by high-affinity binding of HCF-1 peptides in the TPR lumen.

We also assessed global glycosylation activity of the OGT variants by adding them to HeLa cell extracts and immunoblotting for O-GlcNAcylated proteins. Unlike cell lysates, cell extracts are metabolically active, preserving small molecule pools and protein complexes. Cell extracts are useful for assessing the roles of different OGT features in global glycosylation activity because it is possible to control how much OGT is added.30 After incubating 1 μM OGT variant with extract for 15 min, we blotted for O-GlcNAc. OGT-N322A and OGT-N356A both had low O-GlcNAcylation activity compared with N390A, N424A, and N458A, which had wild type-like activity (Figure 3E). Consistent with previous results, OGT-5N5A-1 had very low activity.30,31 Although the results for global glycosylation only partially mirror those for the model substrate HCF3R-SAA, they reinforce the importance of the TPR asparagines in controlling substrate selection. Overall, the results support the emerging view that different OGT substrates are sensitive to different subsets of contacts in the TPR lumen.20,30

### HCF-1 Repeats 1 and 2 Drive High-Affinity Binding of HCF3R

The picomolar binding affinity of OGT-WT for HCF3R-AAA compared with the single-repeat substrate provided evidence that the longer substrate makes additional contacts. The threonine-rich region of a single repeat spans approximately four TPRs. While the repeats in HCF3R are nearly identical, the spacing between repeats varies substantially (Figure 1B). A construct containing the second and third repeats (HCF2R-2/3) would, in principle, be able to span the full TPR domain in an extended conformation. However, a construct containing the first and second repeats (HCF2R-1/2) could only do so if the 36-residue segment between the repeats “looped out” from the TPR lumen. For entropic reasons, one might predict that HCF2R-2/3 would bind better than HCF2R-1/2. To test this prediction, we made both HCF2R constructs with E10A glycosite mutations and measured their KD values in a competition binding assay with probe 1 and saturating UDP. HCF2R-1/2 bound with low nanomolar affinity (KD = 3.5 nM) while HCF2R-2/3 bound less tightly (KD = 51 nM) (Figure 4A). These results imply that HCF3R’s high affinity for OGT cannot be explained by a simple model in which consecutive repeats bind sequentially in the TPR lumen without an intervening unbound region.

### OGT Dimerizes at Midnanomolar Concentrations

OGT is known to homodimerize in vitro,32,39,40 so we considered the possibility that multirepeat HCF-1 constructs might be able to bind simultaneously to two different OGT monomers depending on the linker length. Based on the dimer structure,32,40 the linker between repeats 1 and 2 appears long enough to permit each repeat to bind in the active site and up through the first four TPRs of each monomer. To test whether the repeats can bind simultaneously to both subunits of OGT, we first needed to determine the KD for OGT homodimerization (KD,dimer), which has not previously been measured.

OGT dimerizes via an antiparallel symmetric interface located on the external surface of its sixth and seventh TPRs (Figure 4B), and previous work showed that replacing W198 and I201 with glutamate and aspartate, respectively, prevents dimer formation.39,40 To determine the KD,dimer for OGT-WT, we labeled separate aliquots with either CoraFluor-1-PFP ester or AF488-TFP ester, generating CoraFluor-OGT-WT and AF488-OGT-WT, respectively. We held CoraFluor-OGT-WT constant at 1 nM and added varying amounts of AF488-OGT-WT up to 1 μM and then measured the TR-FRET ratio (Figure 4C). We plotted the binding curve to obtain a KD,dimer of 39 nM for OGT-WT. We repeated this experiment using CoraFluor- and AF488-labeled monomeric OGT (W198E/I201D, OGT-mono) and determined that this mutant has a KD,dimer in excess of 1 μM, the highest OGT concentration tested (Figure 4D). This result is consistent with a previous study that used size exclusion chromatography to show that OGT-mono is monomeric even at millimolar concentrations.40

### Monomeric OGT Binds the Multirepeat Probe with High Affinity

Our binding assays typically use OGT at concentrations below the KD,dimer ([OGT] ≤ 1 nM), where a majority of OGT exists as a monomer. Under these conditions, probe 2 binds UDP-saturated OGT-mono with a KD,app of 0.7 nM, which is less than 10-fold higher than its affinity for OGT-WT (Figure 4E). OGT-mono also cleaves HCF3R-EEE at wild-type levels in vitro (Figure S7). Therefore, OGT’s ability to dimerize is not required for engagement of, or catalytic activity toward, HCF3R. To confirm that HCF3R binding does not depend on OGT dimerization, we repeated the OGT-WT dimerization assay in the presence of UDP while varying the concentration of HCF3R-AAA (Figure S8). If HCF3R binding drives dimer formation by interacting with two copies of OGT, we would expect to observe a decrease in the dimerization constant. However, there was no change in KD,dimer from 0 to 100 nM added HCF3R in the presence of UDP. Therefore, under our binding assay conditions, the three-repeat probe HCF3R binds monomeric OGT regardless of whether the homodimer interface is intact. We have concluded that the much greater affinity of 2 compared with 1, or of HCF2R-1/2 compared with HCF2R-2/3, cannot be explained by simultaneous binding of a single polypeptide to both subunits of an OGT dimer. Instead, our results are consistent with a model in which one HCF-1 polypeptide repeat binds to one OGT, with flanking amino acids and perhaps the second repeat making additional contacts that explain the differences in affinity. Structural studies will be required to better understand how such high-affinity binding is achieved.

### HCF3R-AAA Inhibits OGT In Vitro and in Cells

The unexpectedly high affinity of HCF3R-AAA for wild-type OGT suggested that it might serve as an effective inhibitor of O-GlcNAcylation. Indeed, we found that HCF3R-AAA almost fully inhibited glycosylation in HeLa cell extracts to which wild-type OGT was added in an equimolar ratio (Figure 5A). Therefore, we used lentivirus to integrate a gene encoding a GFP-FLAG fusion of HCF3R-AAA into mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) under the constitutively active PGK promoter. The parent MEF cell line was engineered to contain a degron-tagged copy of OGT, permitting its inducible degradation with the heterobifunctional small molecule dTAG-13 to serve as a control for loss of OGT activity.9,20,41 Following puromycin selection and sorting for high GFP expression, we performed confocal microscopy and found that the construct was present in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm (Figure S9), implying that it is available to inhibit both nuclear and cytoplasmically localized OGT. We then harvested cells and immunoblotted to assess inhibitory activity. An anti-FLAG blot showed good expression of the full-length HCF3R construct, although we also observed likely degradation products. An O-GlcNAc blot showed that glycosylation in cells expressing HCF3R-AAA was reduced to levels nearing the degrader-treated control (Figure 5B). OGT’s ability to cleave HCF-1 was also inhibited by expression of HCF3R (Figure S10). Despite the presence of myriad competing substrates and binding partners, HCF3R-AAA inhibits OGT’s catalytic functions in cells.

### Development of a Chemo-Switchable Cellular OGT Inhibitor

Encouraged by the above results, we turned our attention to creating an inducible OGT inhibitor that could be rapidly degraded. For these studies, we used a human colorectal cancer cell line (HCT116). We made a construct expressing fluorescently tagged HCF3R-AAA as a fusion with the degron FKBP12F36V under the doxycycline-inducible Tet-ON promoter system and integrated it into HCT116 cells using lentivirus (Figure 5C).41−43 Following selection, expression was induced for 24 h by addition of doxycycline and cells were sorted for high GFP levels. As an initial test of our dual induction/degradation system, we performed fixed-cell confocal microscopy on cells either treated with no compound, doxycycline for 24 h, or the small molecule dTAGV-1 (see note in Methods) for 24 h after a 24 h doxycycline treatment (Figure S11). While the images indicate heterogeneous expression, which may be a byproduct of our fixation conditions, they demonstrate a clear on–off switch for HCF3R levels induced by addition of doxycycline and dTAGV-1.

To fine-tune our system and determine the impact of HCF3R on OGT activity, we performed two separate time-course experiments with western blot visualization. In the first experiment, we varied the length of doxycycline treatment to induce HCF3R expression. Here, we found that HCF3R was detectable beginning at 4 h of induction, but maximal at 24 h, at which point O-GlcNAc levels were reduced compared with those in the untreated sample (Figure 5D, left). The inhibitory effects were not as dramatic as in the MEFs, but overall glycosylation levels were relatively low under our growth conditions even before HCF3R expression. Under these conditions we did not observe any changes in HCF-1 cleavage (Figure S12), however, we anticipate that at longer time points, uncleaved HCF-1 would accumulate, consistent with previous studies of OGT inhibition.9,35

In the second experiment, we treated the modified HCT116 cells with doxycycline for 24 h, then conducted a time course of degradation after adding dTAGV-1 to determine if the induction phenotypes were reversible. We found that HCF3R was rapidly degraded; after 2 h of degradation, signal was nearly undetectable (Figure 5D, right). Concurrent with degradation, O-GlcNAcylation rapidly recovered, peaking within 2 h and remaining elevated for at least 6 h before decreasing to basal levels by 24 h. The high O-GlcNAc levels observed when the inhibitor is abruptly degraded likely reflect compensatory mechanisms that buffer low cellular O-GlcNAc. One such mechanism involves altering levels of OGT and its counterpart glycosidase OGA.32 Because OGT and OGA levels were not dramatically altered in the presence of HCF3R (Figure S12), we do not think this mechanism fully explains the dramatic rebound glycosylation immediately following HCF3R degradation. Further studies on this rebound phenomenon using our on–off system may uncover additional regulatory mechanisms that control cellular O-GlcNAc levels.

## Discussion

Here, we developed a TR-FRET assay to comprehensively profile and characterize OGT’s binding interactions and applied it to understand the features in OGT that drive binding of its most prominent interactor, HCF-1. In this work, we identified an HCF-1-derived polypeptide that is a picomolar binder, which we exploited to assess the contribution of the nucleotide cofactor and residues in OGT’s TPR domain to substrate binding. We found that conserved TPR asparagines can contribute as much as 7 kcal/mol to the binding affinity of an OGT ligand, a finding with implications for de novo design of protein receptor–ligand pairs. We also used our assay to provide the first quantitative measurement of the KD for OGT homodimerization, information necessary for evaluating whether OGT functions as a dimer in cells. Finally, we have demonstrated that HCF-1-derived polypeptides can serve as genetically encoded inhibitors to manipulate OGT activity in cells, making them useful for studies in which the available small molecular inhibitors cannot be used.

HCF-1 has been consistently identified as OGT’s most prevalent binding partner across the literature, with an early study showing that ∼50% of OGT is complexed to HCF-1.19−21 OGT cleaves the repeat region of HCF-1, but the two halves of the cleaved protein remain associated following cleavage.44,45 Failure to cleave HCF-1 is reported to cause mitotic defects.28 Given that the N- and C-terminal fragments of HCF-1 remain associated, it is unclear why its cleavage is necessary. One study has suggested that the repeat region of HCF-1 binds other proteins and that cleavage by OGT controls interaction of these proteins with HCF-1.24 Evidence suggests that OGT binds full-length HCF-1 more strongly than its cleavage products, raising the possibility that cleavage, which is dependent on UDP-GlcNAc, regulates binding of OGT to HCF-1 as a mechanism to regulate OGT’s interactions with other binding partners or substrates. Understanding how interaction with HCF-1 affects OGT’s biology is an important area to address in future work.

The subnanomolar affinity of OGT for HCF3R-AAA was unexpected, as this polypeptide is unstructured and lacks both charged residues for salt bridges and prolines to constrain conformation, factors typically associated with high-affinity binding. In nature, protein motifs with repeating elements that bind extended peptides via bidentate contacts to their backbones are common. In addition to OGT, examples include tetratricopeptide repeats in other proteins, and armadillo repeats in proteins such as importin-α.46−48 These repeat proteins have attracted interest in the protein design field as starting points for artificial receptors because binding affinities can be modulated by addition or removal of repeats, and selectivity can be tuned using multiple repeats that vary in specified ways.47,49,50 The peptide ligands typically used in these studies contain rigidifying prolines, and amino acid frequency plots of OGT substrates indicate that the majority of them also contain prolines in regions predicted to bind OGT’s TPR domain.12,51,52 The presence of prolines can affect substrate binding affinity positively or negatively: prolines can not only reduce entropic penalties to binding, but also disrupt bidentate interactions because the tertiary proline amide cannot act as a hydrogen bond donor. Thus, incorporation of prolines at positions that would otherwise make bidentate contacts to OGT’s conserved asparagines would disrupt the bidentate hydrogen bonding network.32 In addition, torsional constraints due to proline incorporation may change the orientation of flanking residues, thereby affecting their interactions. We showed with our model glycosylation substrate (HCF3R-SAA) that very high-affinity binding to OGT’s TPR lumen can limit turnover of glycosylation substrates. For OGT’s native glycosylation substrates, incorporation of prolines that disrupt bidentate interactions may serve as a mechanism to tune TPR binding interactions for optimal turnover.

HCF-1, unlike many OGT glycosylation substrates, does not contain prolines in the TPR binding region of its repeats. Instead, OGT’s conserved TPR asparagines anchor HCF-1’s repeats using an uninterrupted series of bidentate hydrogen bonds to every other residue along the amide backbone. We could not find any data in the literature on the energetic contributions of bidentate hydrogen bonds between side chain and backbone amides in receptor-ligand pairs, even though such interactions have been exploited in de novo design.50 We showed in this study that replacing individual OGT asparagine ladder residues with alanines decreased binding of HCF3R-AAA by at least 5 orders of magnitude. Without a very high-affinity ligand, we could not have observed this dramatic change in binding. Some of the decrease in affinity may be due to reduced desolvation entropy: removal of an asparagine side chain would leave space for bound waters that are not displaced upon binding. However, a substantial portion of the binding energy is likely derived from hydrogen bonds. Applying an analysis formulated by Jencks,53,54 we suggest that formation of the first H-bond in each of these bidentate interactions helps counteract losses in OGT side chain conformational entropy so that the intrinsic value of the second hydrogen bond is fully realized. Successive asparagine-backbone contacts also help orient the backbone conformation of the ligand, in turn facilitating formation of the adjacent bidentate hydrogen bonds. In other words, we think substantial cooperativity in the hydrogen bonding network explains the high affinity and the dramatic loss in binding that occurs with removal of any individual asparagine side chain.

Our study has also determined the KD value for OGT dimerization, providing crucial insights into how dimerization influences OGT’s cellular functions. OGT’s dimer interface was identified in 2004,39 but the functional consequences of dimerization are still unclear. It has been shown for two substrates that in vitro glycosylation activity decreases substantially when the dimer interface is disrupted.32,40 It was therefore suggested that OGT functions as an obligate dimer in cells. We recently showed that monomeric OGT can support cell growth when wild-type OGT is deleted, indicating that the dimer interface is not essential for viability in tissue culture.20 The KD value we determined for OGT dimerization (39 nM) is below estimated cellular OGT concentrations (∼100 nM),55 but high enough that some monomeric OGT would be expected to exist in cells. Disruption of the dimer interface can affect substrate glycosylation, suggesting that monomeric and dimeric populations of OGT exist in cells and can have distinct biologically relevant activities. However, this possibility should be addressed in future work.

While we continue investigating the molecular basis for HCF3R-AAA’s remarkable affinity for OGT, future structural studies will likely be needed for deeper insights. Meanwhile, we have leveraged this high affinity to develop a genetically encoded OGT inhibitor. We found that expressing HCF3R-AAA in cells inhibits O-GlcNAcylation and, if expressed constitutively, can also inhibit HCF-1 cleavage. Therefore, the HCF3R-AAA polypeptide effectively competes for binding with both endogenous HCF-1 and with OGT’s numerous glycosylation substrates. We have demonstrated that this polypeptide inhibitor can be inducibly expressed, and that we can achieve reversibility of inhibition by incorporation of a degron tag. Further optimization may be necessary, but our results demonstrate the promise of genetically encoded OGT inhibitors. We suggest that such inhibitors will be particularly useful in animal models where the current suite of small molecule OGT inhibitors has major limitations.
